analysis.one_liner: Sets uniform federal safety standards and tougher oversight for interstate motorcoach buses.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; it was referred to four House committees on February 23, 2009 and received no further action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The BUSES Act would have required the Transportation Department to write the first federal crash-protection standards for motorcoaches, covering seat belts, roof strength, window glazing, fire prevention, and emergency exits for both new and existing buses. It also would have tightened oversight of bus companies: monitoring carrier safety records, setting minimum training for drivers, screening medical examiners who certify drivers, and closing a loophole that let operators with unsafe records reappear under new ownership. To ease the cost, it offered small bus operators a tax credit, retrofit grants up to $20,000 per vehicle, and Small Business Administration loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of Americans who ride interstate and charter buses, including low-income travelers, students, seniors, and workers commuting between cities, would gain stronger protection in crashes: seat belts, crush-resistant roofs, ejection-proof windows, fire safeguards, and trained, medically screened drivers. Legitimate bus companies would also gain from a tax credit, retrofit grants up to $20,000 per bus, and SBA loans to help pay for the upgrades, while facing less competition from operators who skirt safety rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bus passengers and small bus operators

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Transportation Department to prescribe federal motor vehicle safety standards for motorcoach occupant protection covering frontal, side, rear impact, and rollover crashes, plus roof strength, window glazing, fire prevention, and emergency evacuation design [S2] [S3].
Requires the Department to set minimum training requirements for drivers seeking a commercial license passenger endorsement and to review passenger-endorsement testing requirements [S2] [S3].

Directs the Secretary to establish and enforce requirements for medical examiners who certify commercial drivers' physical fitness, including a national registry with a rigorous examination and annual reviews of at least 10 states' implementation [S2] [S3].

Requires sustained monitoring of each passenger motor carrier's safety performance with progressive interventions and enforcement, including strike forces to target unsafe operators, and lets the Secretary deny or revoke the registration of companies that dodge safety rules by changing names or ownership [S2] [S3].

Offsets compliance costs for small operators with a tax credit of up to $45,000 per qualifying motorcoach, retrofit grants up to $20,000 per vehicle, and SBA loans and loan guarantees targeted at the charter bus industry [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the retrofit grants and bear the cost of any tax credits claimed, and bus companies would pay to upgrade or replace buses on the mandated multi-year timetable, a cost they could pass on to riders through ticket prices. The federal government would also spend more on inspections, driver oversight, and rulemaking.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on motorcoach operators, many of them small businesses, and even with the credit, grants, and loans, higher costs could be passed to riders as higher ticket prices [S2] [S3].
The bill authorizes appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' for grants and enforcement without capping the total cost to taxpayers [S3].

The bill preempts states from adopting their own motorcoach safety rules during the phase-in period, and several of its key steps are studies and reviews rather than immediate requirements, so safety gains would arrive years after enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case was strong: buses carry tens of millions of passengers with, at the time, no federal seat belt or roof-crush standards, and the NTSB had recommended such rules for a decade. The bill tried to soften the cost on small operators with credits, grants, and loans, though it left the total taxpayer cost open-ended and the standards would have taken years to phase in.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee its entire life: after introduction it was referred to four House committees, its subcommittees never acted, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011 without ever reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Representative Bill Shuster, joined by Representative Eddie Bernice Johnson of Texas, introduced the bill in the House on February 23, 2009 [S1] [S3].
It was referred to four House committees at once: Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Small Business [S1] [S5].
On February 23 and 24, 2009, it was referred to three subcommittees: Regulations, Health Care, and Trade; Highways and Transit; and Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no version was introduced in the Senate, and no floor vote ever occurred; the Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died there [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unsafe or marginal bus operators kept operating under the old rules, avoiding retrofit costs and closer federal monitoring, while bus riders remained without the federal seat belt, roof-strength, and ejection protections the bill would have required. Small legitimate operators also missed the tax credits, grants, and loans the bill offered to offset compliance costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unsafe operators and riders without new protections

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start, with a Republican sponsor and original cosponsor joined by 4 more Democrats and 5 Republicans, so the bill's failure was not a partisan vote but a committee that never acted.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed retrofit and compliance costs on bus companies but offset them for small operators with tax credits up to $45,000 per bus, grants up to $20,000 per vehicle, and SBA loans, while undercutting unsafe competitors through tighter registration and monitoring [S2] [S3].
New federal safety standards for new and existing coaches would drive demand for compliant new buses and retrofit equipment, a cost offset by the bill's tax credit [S3].
Taxpayer exposure includes the retrofit grant program, SBA loan guarantees, and uncapped appropriations, alongside open-ended tax credits for compliant bus purchases [S3].
